title: DuckLake or Iceberg?

rows.label: In one line
values: Table metadata as rows in a SQL database, data as Parquet files
Table metadata as a tree of JSON and Avro files next to the data, found through a catalog

rows.label: Where metadata lives
values: Ordinary tables in a catalog database: PostgreSQL for many users, SQLite or a DuckDB file locally; MySQL works but isn’t recommended
Files in object storage: a metadata JSON file, manifest lists and Avro manifests; the catalog stores only the location of the current metadata file

rows.label: Commit path
values: One database transaction. Snapshot ids are a primary key, so of two clashing writers one fails, then retries without rewriting data files unless the changes really conflict
Write data files and new metadata files, then swap the catalog’s pointer atomically; if another commit got there first, retry against the new snapshot

rows.label: Changes across tables
values: Atomic, through the database’s own transactions
Atomic only through a REST catalog’s multi-table commit endpoint, where the catalog implements it

rows.label: Small writes
values: Inlined: inserts and deletes of up to 10 rows by default are stored in the catalog database and flushed to Parquet later, for example by `CHECKPOINT`
Every commit writes at least one data file plus new metadata files, so frequent small commits pile up files until compaction runs

rows.label: Deletes and updates
values: A positional delete file in Parquet per affected data file; deletion vectors in Puffin files are experimental in 1.0
Copy-on-write rewrites, or merge-on-read with position or equality delete files (v2) and deletion vectors in Puffin files (v3)

rows.label: Catalog
values: The catalog database is the catalog; there is no separate service to run
A separate catalog to choose and run: a REST catalog such as Polaris or Lakekeeper, AWS Glue, Nessie or a JDBC database

rows.label: Engines
values: DuckDB’s `ducklake` extension is the reference; DataFusion, Spark (from MotherDuck) and two Trino implementations come from others
Spark, Flink, Trino, DuckDB, ClickHouse, Snowflake, BigQuery, Athena, Redshift and many more

rows.label: Maintenance
values: Merge adjacent files, expire snapshots, delete old files and rewrite files with many deletes; `CHECKPOINT` runs them together. Vacuum the catalog database now and then
Compact data files, rewrite delete files, expire snapshots and remove orphan files, on a schedule or through a managed service

rows.label: What limits scale
values: The catalog database’s performance, according to the FAQ
Metadata reads and commit conflicts: many snapshots and manifests slow planning, and many writers to one table retry

rows.label: Interoperability
values: Copies tables to and from Iceberg since 0.3; bucket partitioning uses Iceberg’s murmur3 hashing
XTable can translate its metadata to and from Delta Lake and Hudi

rows.label: Maturity
values: Announced in May 2025; 1.0 in April 2026 with a backward-compatibility guarantee
Started at Netflix in 2017, Apache top-level project since 2020; spec versions 1 to 3 complete, 4 in development

rows.label: Licence and governance
values: MIT, for both the spec and the DuckDB extension; developed by the DuckDB team
Apache 2.0; an Apache Software Foundation project

tip: Pick DuckLake when DuckDB is your main engine and you already run PostgreSQL: there is no catalog service, small writes are cheap and multi-table transactions come free. Pick Iceberg when many engines and cloud services must read and write the same tables. The choice isn’t final: both keep data as Parquet, and DuckLake can copy tables out to Iceberg.
